Code illustration 6.1 · stats_engine_part1.py — mean, median and range by hand, checked against the oracle

Task
The program defines StatsEngine with mean, median and value_range, each with a guard; it runs them on the fun-quiz list [4, 9, 1, 7] (showing the wrong value you get without sorting), then on the 55 manual e-mail runs of the dataset, prints two validation rows against the statistics module and finishes by catching the ValueError of an empty list.
Relation to the lecture
Every step is a sentence of Lesson 6.1: the static methods and the guard (6.1.2), the sorted copy and the odd/even rule (6.1.3), the naming rule and the validation rows (6.1.4). The numbers it prints are the ones of Real-life example 6.1.

1# -*- coding: utf-8 -*-
2# The module docstring: it states what this file is for, so that anyone who opens it knows its purpose.
3"""CS 251 - Class 6 - Lesson 6.1: StatsEngine, part 1 - mean, median and value_range, written by hand.
4
5The engine is yours: it must not call statistics.mean or statistics.median inside its methods.
6The statistics module of the standard library is the ORACLE: it is used only to check the engine.
7"""
8
9# The csv module reads the dataset one row at a time, as dictionaries keyed by the header line.
10import csv
11# math.isclose compares two floating-point results with a tolerance (Lesson 6.2 explains why == is the wrong question).
12import math
13# The statistics module is imported ONLY as the oracle (the reference answer) - never inside the engine.
14import statistics
15# pathlib.Path builds a file path that works on Windows, macOS and Linux without a hard-coded folder.
16from pathlib import Path
17
18# The dataset lives in the data/ folder next to the code/ folder: no absolute path, no C:\Users\... anywhere.
19DATA = Path(__file__).resolve().parent.parent / "data" / "boreal_routines_2026.csv"
20
21
22# A class groups the statistics methods under one name; the engine has no state, so its methods are static.
23class StatsEngine:
24    # The class docstring says what the class owns: the descriptive statistics of a list of numbers.
25    """Descriptive statistics of a list of numbers (part 1: mean, median, value_range)."""
26
27    # @staticmethod means the method needs no object and no self: StatsEngine.mean([...]) is enough.
28    @staticmethod
29    # mean takes a list of numbers and returns one number; the type hints document that contract.
30    def mean(xs: list[float]) -> float:
31        # The docstring states the formula, so the method is its own documentation (and its own test oracle).
32        """Arithmetic mean: sum of the values divided by their count. Empty list -> ValueError."""
33        # An empty list has no mean: refusing with a clear message is better than a ZeroDivisionError later.
34        if not xs:
35            # raise stops the method here and hands the problem to the caller, with the reason in words.
36            raise ValueError("mean of an empty list is undefined")
37        # sum() adds all the values, len() counts them; the division gives the mean in one line.
38        return sum(xs) / len(xs)
39
40    # Again a static method: median needs only the list.
41    @staticmethod
42    # median returns the middle value of the SORTED values; for an even count, the average of the two middles.
43    def median(xs: list[float]) -> float:
44        # The docstring repeats the rule, including the even case, so the reader never has to guess.
45        """Median: middle of the sorted values (odd n) or the average of the two middle values (even n)."""
46        # The same guard as for mean: no values, no median.
47        if not xs:
48            # A clear message again; the test in Class 10 will expect exactly this exception type.
49            raise ValueError("median of an empty list is undefined")
50        # sorted() returns a NEW sorted list and leaves xs untouched; xs.sort() would reorder the caller's data.
51        ordered = sorted(xs)
52        # n is the number of values; it decides whether there is one middle value or two.
53        n = len(ordered)
54        # Integer division by 2 gives the index of the middle (odd n) or of the upper middle (even n).
55        mid = n // 2
56        # The remainder of n divided by 2 is 1 for an odd count: one middle value.
57        if n % 2 == 1:
58            # The middle element of the sorted copy is the median.
59            return ordered[mid]
60        # For an even count the median is the mean of the two values around the middle.
61        return (ordered[mid - 1] + ordered[mid]) / 2
62
63    # The third static method of part 1: the range of the values.
64    @staticmethod
65    # value_range is named so because range() is a built-in function of Python: a method called range would hide it.
66    def value_range(xs: list[float]) -> float:
67        # The docstring: largest value minus smallest value.
68        """Range: largest value minus smallest value. Empty list -> ValueError."""
69        # The guard once more: max() and min() of an empty list would raise their own, less clear, error.
70        if not xs:
71            # Same exception type as the other methods, so the tests can treat the three the same way.
72            raise ValueError("range of an empty list is undefined")
73        # max() and min() scan the list; their difference is the range.
74        return max(xs) - min(xs)
75
76
77# A helper function reads the minutes of one routine done with one tool (for example manual e-mail triage).
78def load_minutes(routine: str, tool: str) -> list[int]:
79    # The docstring explains the filter: routine and tool must both match.
80    """Minutes of every run of one routine done with one tool, read from the teaching dataset."""
81    # The with statement opens the file and closes it automatically; newline="" is required by the csv module.
82    with DATA.open(newline="", encoding="utf-8") as f:
83        # DictReader yields one dict per row; the comprehension keeps the minutes of the matching rows as int.
84        return [int(row["minutes"]) for row in csv.DictReader(f) if row["routine"] == routine and row["tool"] == tool]
85
86
87# A small list first: it is the list of the fun quiz, and small enough to check by hand.
88small = [4, 9, 1, 7]
89# The engine's median of the small list: sorted copy [1, 4, 7, 9], two middles 4 and 7, average 5.5.
90print("median of", small, "=", StatsEngine.median(small))
91# The caller's list must be unchanged after the call: sorted() made a copy, it did not sort in place.
92print("the list after the call:", small)
93# The trap of the fun quiz: taking the two middle values WITHOUT sorting gives (9 + 1) / 2 = 5.0, which is wrong.
94unsorted_middle = (small[len(small) // 2 - 1] + small[len(small) // 2]) / 2
95# Print the wrong value next to the right one so that the difference is visible.
96print("the same two positions without sorting:", unsorted_middle, "(wrong)")
97# The oracle: statistics.median must agree with the engine on the small list.
98print("oracle statistics.median:", statistics.median(small))
99
100# Now the real data: every manual run of e-mail triage in the 14 days (55 runs, the worked example of Class 4).
101email = load_minutes("email_triage", "manual")
102# The count of values; it must be 55 (5 staff x 14 days minus the 15 pilot runs done with the assistant).
103print("manual e-mail triage runs:", len(email))
104# The engine's mean of the 55 runs, rounded to two decimals for the report.
105print(f"mean   = {StatsEngine.mean(email):.2f} min")
106# The engine's median: the middle of the sorted copy (n = 55 is odd, so it is the 28th value).
107print(f"median = {StatsEngine.median(email):.2f} min")
108# The engine's range: longest run minus shortest run.
109print(f"range  = {StatsEngine.value_range(email)} min")
110
111# The validation habit of Class 6: the engine's value next to the oracle's value, and whether they match.
112for name, ours, oracle in [("mean", StatsEngine.mean(email), statistics.mean(email)), ("median", StatsEngine.median(email), statistics.median(email))]:
113    # A row of the validation table: name, engine value, oracle value, and the verdict - compared with a tolerance, never with ==.
114    print(f"{name:<8}{ours:>8.2f}{oracle:>8.2f}  {'match' if math.isclose(ours, oracle) else 'DIFFERENT'}")
115
116# The guard in action: an empty list must raise ValueError, not crash with ZeroDivisionError.
117try:
118    # This call cannot succeed; the except branch below receives the exception.
119    StatsEngine.mean([])
120# The exception is caught here and its message is printed - the program continues normally.
121except ValueError as error:
122    # The message written in the engine appears here, exactly as the test of Class 10 will expect it.
123    print("empty list ->", type(error).__name__, "-", error)

    Step by step — what the program does

    1. Imports and the data path. csv reads the dataset, statistics is imported only as the oracle, math for isclose, and Path(__file__).resolve().parent.parent / "data" / ... finds the CSV (Comma-Separated Values) file relative to the code folder — no absolute path anywhere.
    2. The class. StatsEngine has three static methods. Watch the variables panel: nothing is stored on the class; each call works only with its argument xs.
    3. median on the small list. ordered = sorted(small) creates [1, 4, 7, 9]; n = 4, mid = 2; the even branch returns (4 + 7) / 2 = 5.5. The next line prints small unchanged — the sorted copy did its job.
    4. The trap. unsorted_middle takes positions 1 and 2 of the unsorted list: (9 + 1) / 2 = 5.0. No error, wrong number.
    5. The real data. load_minutes("email_triage", "manual") keeps the 55 rows whose routine and tool match; the three methods return 35.15, 35.00 and 26.
    6. Validation rows. The for loop prints mean and median with the engine's value, the oracle's value and match; the verdict comes from math.isclose, never from ==. Note the format specs :<8 and :>8.2f — Lesson 6.4 explains them.
    7. The guard in action. StatsEngine.mean([]) raises inside the method (the exception event appears in the steps list), the except ValueError as error branch catches it and prints the message. The program ends normally.

    Code illustration 6.2 · stats_engine_part2.py — mode, variance, SD, CV (coefficient of variation), quartiles and the two outlier rules

    Task
    The program adds the spread methods to StatsEngine — mode with a documented tie rule, variance and std_dev with n − 1, cv, inclusive quartiles, iqr, outliers (1.5 × IQR (interquartile range)) and outliers_sd (mean ± 2 s) — checks Set A by hand against statistics.stdev and pstdev, shows the floating-point trap and math.isclose, then runs everything on the 55 manual e-mail runs.
    Relation to the lecture
    Every step is a sentence of Lesson 6.2: the Counter and the tie (6.2.1), n − 1 (6.2.2), the CV (coefficient of variation) (6.2.3), isclose (6.2.4), the quartile positions and the fences (6.2.5). The numbers it prints are the ones of Real-life example 6.2 and of six rows of the validation table.

    1# -*- coding: utf-8 -*-
    2# The module docstring: part 2 of the engine - the spread of the values and the outliers.
    3"""CS 251 - Class 6 - Lesson 6.2: StatsEngine, part 2 - mode, variance, standard deviation, CV, quartiles, IQR, outliers.
    4
    5Conventions decided in Class 4 and kept by the engine:
    6  * sample variance and standard deviation divide by n - 1 (our 14 days are a sample, not the whole year)
    7  * mode returns the LIST of all tied values, sorted (a tie is information, not an error)
    8  * quartiles use the inclusive method (statistics.quantiles(..., method="inclusive"), QUARTILE.INC, NumPy's default)
    9  * floating-point results are compared with a tolerance (math.isclose), never with ==
    10"""
    11
    12# csv reads the dataset; the helper that loads one routine is the same as in part 1.
    13import csv
    14# math gives sqrt (the standard deviation is the square root of the variance) and isclose (float comparison).
    15import math
    16# statistics is the oracle again: the reference values the engine is checked against.
    17import statistics
    18# Counter counts how many times each value occurs - exactly what the mode needs.
    19from collections import Counter
    20# Path finds the data folder relative to this file, on every operating system.
    21from pathlib import Path
    22
    23# The teaching dataset of Classes 3 to 6: 420 rows, one per routine run.
    24DATA = Path(__file__).resolve().parent.parent / "data" / "boreal_routines_2026.csv"
    25
    26
    27# The engine class of part 2; part 1 (mean, median, value_range) is in stats_engine_part1.py.
    28class StatsEngine:
    29    # The class docstring names the conventions once more, where a reader of the code will look.
    30    """Descriptive statistics, part 2: spread and outliers (sample conventions, n - 1)."""
    31
    32    # mean is repeated here because variance needs it (in the real package both live in one class).
    33    @staticmethod
    34    # The same mean as in part 1: sum divided by count, empty list refused.
    35    def mean(xs: list[float]) -> float:
    36        # Docstring: the formula.
    37        """Arithmetic mean; empty list -> ValueError."""
    38        # Guard against the empty list.
    39        if not xs:
    40            # Clear message, same exception type everywhere in the engine.
    41            raise ValueError("mean of an empty list is undefined")
    42        # One line does the work.
    43        return sum(xs) / len(xs)
    44
    45    # The mode: the most frequent value(s).
    46    @staticmethod
    47    # mode returns a list, because several values can share the highest count.
    48    def mode(xs: list[float]) -> list[float]:
    49        # The docstring documents the tie decision - the reader must not have to discover it by surprise.
    50        """Most frequent value(s). Ties: ALL tied values are returned, sorted. Empty list -> ValueError."""
    51        # Guard.
    52        if not xs:
    53            # Message.
    54            raise ValueError("mode of an empty list is undefined")
    55        # Counter maps each value to its number of occurrences, e.g. {29: 5, 32: 5, 37: 5, 30: 4, ...}.
    56        counts = Counter(xs)
    57        # The highest count; most_common(1) returns a list with one (value, count) pair.
    58        top = counts.most_common(1)[0][1]
    59        # Every value whose count equals the highest count is a mode; sorted() makes the answer deterministic.
    60        return sorted(value for value, count in counts.items() if count == top)
    61
    62    # The sample variance.
    63    @staticmethod
    64    # variance divides by n - 1: the sample convention of Class 4.
    65    def variance(xs: list[float]) -> float:
    66        # Docstring with the formula and the n - 1 convention, which the Mid-Term will ask about.
    67        """Sample variance: sum of squared deviations from the mean divided by (n - 1). Needs at least 2 values."""
    68        # Two values are the minimum: with one value, n - 1 = 0 and the division is impossible.
    69        if len(xs) < 2:
    70            # The message says what the method needs.
    71            raise ValueError("variance needs at least two values")
    72        # The mean is computed once and reused in the sum.
    73        m = StatsEngine.mean(xs)
    74        # Each deviation (x - m) is squared and summed; the sum is divided by n - 1 (not n: this is a sample).
    75        return sum((x - m) ** 2 for x in xs) / (len(xs) - 1)
    76
    77    # The sample standard deviation.
    78    @staticmethod
    79    # std_dev is the square root of the sample variance, in the same unit as the data (minutes).
    80    def std_dev(xs: list[float]) -> float:
    81        # Docstring.
    82        """Sample standard deviation: square root of the sample variance."""
    83        # math.sqrt returns a float; the variance method already guards the input.
    84        return math.sqrt(StatsEngine.variance(xs))
    85
    86    # The coefficient of variation.
    87    @staticmethod
    88    # cv compares the spread of routines of different length: standard deviation divided by the mean.
    89    def cv(xs: list[float]) -> float:
    90        # Docstring: it is a ratio (0.181), printed later as a percentage (18.1 %).
    91        """Coefficient of variation: std_dev / mean, as a ratio (multiply by 100 for a percentage). Mean 0 -> ValueError."""
    92        # The mean is the denominator; a mean of zero would make the ratio meaningless.
    93        m = StatsEngine.mean(xs)
    94        # Guard against division by zero.
    95        if m == 0:
    96            # Message.
    97            raise ValueError("cv is undefined when the mean is 0")
    98        # The ratio.
    99        return StatsEngine.std_dev(xs) / m
    100
    101    # The quartiles, inclusive method (the same values as statistics.quantiles(method="inclusive") and Excel's QUARTILE.INC).
    102    @staticmethod
    103    # quartiles returns the three cut points Q1, Q2 (= median) and Q3.
    104    def quartiles(xs: list[float]) -> tuple[float, float, float]:
    105        # Docstring explains the inclusive rule: position (n - 1) * p in the sorted copy, interpolated.
    106        """Q1, Q2, Q3 by the inclusive method: position (n - 1) * p in the sorted copy, linear interpolation."""
    107        # Guard: at least two values are needed to interpolate.
    108        if len(xs) < 2:
    109            # Message.
    110            raise ValueError("quartiles need at least two values")
    111        # A sorted COPY again - the caller's list is left as it is.
    112        ordered = sorted(xs)
    113        # n - 1 is the distance between the first and the last position.
    114        last = len(ordered) - 1
    115        # An inner helper: the value at a fractional position, interpolated between its two neighbours.
    116        def at(p: float) -> float:
    117            # The exact (possibly fractional) position of the quartile.
    118            pos = last * p
    119            # The whole part of the position: the index of the lower neighbour.
    120            lo = int(pos)
    121            # The fractional part: how far between the lower and the upper neighbour.
    122            frac = pos - lo
    123            # If the position is a whole number, the value is exactly the element there.
    124            if frac == 0:
    125                # Return it as is.
    126                return ordered[lo]
    127            # Otherwise interpolate: lower value plus the fraction of the gap to the upper value.
    128            return ordered[lo] + frac * (ordered[lo + 1] - ordered[lo])
    129        # The three quartiles at positions 0.25, 0.50 and 0.75.
    130        return at(0.25), at(0.50), at(0.75)
    131
    132    # The interquartile range.
    133    @staticmethod
    134    # iqr is Q3 minus Q1: the width of the middle half of the data.
    135    def iqr(xs: list[float]) -> float:
    136        # Docstring.
    137        """Interquartile range: Q3 - Q1."""
    138        # Unpack the three quartiles; Q2 is not needed here.
    139        q1, _, q3 = StatsEngine.quartiles(xs)
    140        # The width.
    141        return q3 - q1
    142
    143    # The outlier rule of Class 4, stated explicitly: the 1.5 x IQR fences.
    144    @staticmethod
    145    # outliers returns the values outside the fences; k = 1.5 is the usual factor, and it is a parameter so the report can say which one was used.
    146    def outliers(xs: list[float], k: float = 1.5) -> list[float]:
    147        # Docstring: the rule in words.
    148        """Values below Q1 - k * IQR or above Q3 + k * IQR (default k = 1.5), in their original order."""
    149        # The quartiles of the sorted copy.
    150        q1, _, q3 = StatsEngine.quartiles(xs)
    151        # The interquartile range.
    152        spread = q3 - q1
    153        # The lower fence.
    154        low = q1 - k * spread
    155        # The upper fence.
    156        high = q3 + k * spread
    157        # Every value outside the fences is an outlier under this rule.
    158        return [x for x in xs if x < low or x > high]
    159
    160    # The second rule of Class 4: mean plus or minus z standard deviations.
    161    @staticmethod
    162    # outliers_sd flags values farther than z standard deviations from the mean (default z = 2).
    163    def outliers_sd(xs: list[float], z: float = 2.0) -> list[float]:
    164        # Docstring.
    165        """Values outside mean +/- z * std_dev (default z = 2), in their original order."""
    166        # The centre.
    167        m = StatsEngine.mean(xs)
    168        # The spread.
    169        s = StatsEngine.std_dev(xs)
    170        # Values beyond z standard deviations on either side.
    171        return [x for x in xs if abs(x - m) > z * s]
    172
    173
    174# The same loader as in part 1.
    175def load_minutes(routine: str, tool: str) -> list[int]:
    176    # Docstring.
    177    """Minutes of every run of one routine done with one tool."""
    178    # Open, read, filter, close - all in one with block.
    179    with DATA.open(newline="", encoding="utf-8") as f:
    180        # The minutes column as integers, for the rows that match.
    181        return [int(row["minutes"]) for row in csv.DictReader(f) if row["routine"] == routine and row["tool"] == tool]
    182
    183
    184# Set A of Class 4: five numbers small enough to check by hand (s^2 = 2.5, s = 1.581).
    185set_a = [8, 10, 9, 12, 11]
    186# The engine's sample variance: deviations -2, 0, -1, 2, 1 -> squares 4, 0, 1, 4, 1 -> sum 10 -> 10 / (5 - 1) = 2.5.
    187print("set A variance (n - 1) =", StatsEngine.variance(set_a))
    188# The sample standard deviation: sqrt(2.5) = 1.5811...
    189print(f"set A std_dev = {StatsEngine.std_dev(set_a):.3f}")
    190# The oracle for the sample SD is statistics.stdev (n - 1); statistics.pstdev would divide by n and give 1.414.
    191print(f"oracle statistics.stdev = {statistics.stdev(set_a):.3f}   (pstdev, n, would give {statistics.pstdev(set_a):.3f})")
    192
    193# The float trap: two floats that are mathematically equal can differ in the last binary digit.
    194print("0.1 + 0.2 == 0.3 ?", 0.1 + 0.2 == 0.3, "->", 0.1 + 0.2)
    195# math.isclose compares with a tolerance: this is how the validation table and the tests must compare floats.
    196print("math.isclose(0.1 + 0.2, 0.3) ?", math.isclose(0.1 + 0.2, 0.3))
    197
    198# The worked example: the 55 manual runs of e-mail triage.
    199email = load_minutes("email_triage", "manual")
    200# The mode: three values tie with five runs each -> the engine returns all three.
    201print("mode (ties kept) =", StatsEngine.mode(email))
    202# The oracle for ties: statistics.multimode returns the same values; statistics.mode would return only the first seen.
    203print("oracle statistics.multimode =", statistics.multimode(email))
    204# Variance and standard deviation of the 55 runs (n - 1).
    205print(f"variance = {StatsEngine.variance(email):.2f}   std_dev = {StatsEngine.std_dev(email):.2f} min")
    206# The coefficient of variation as a percentage: :.1% multiplies by 100 and adds the sign.
    207print(f"cv = {StatsEngine.cv(email):.1%}")
    208# The engine's standard deviation compared with the oracle with == (False: the two floats differ in their last digit)...
    209print("std_dev == statistics.stdev ?", StatsEngine.std_dev(email) == statistics.stdev(email), "->", StatsEngine.std_dev(email), "vs", statistics.stdev(email))
    210# ...and with a tolerance (True): this is the comparison the validation table and the tests use.
    211print("math.isclose(std_dev, statistics.stdev) ?", math.isclose(StatsEngine.std_dev(email), statistics.stdev(email)))
    212# The three quartiles by the inclusive method.
    213q1, q2, q3 = StatsEngine.quartiles(email)
    214# Printed with the oracle: statistics.quantiles with method="inclusive" gives the same three numbers.
    215print(f"quartiles = ({q1}, {q2}, {q3})   oracle inclusive = {statistics.quantiles(email, n=4, method='inclusive')}")
    216# The interquartile range and the two fences of the 1.5 x IQR rule.
    217print(f"IQR = {StatsEngine.iqr(email)}   fences = [{q1 - 1.5 * StatsEngine.iqr(email)}, {q3 + 1.5 * StatsEngine.iqr(email)}]")
    218# Under the IQR rule no run of the 55 is an outlier.
    219print("outliers (1.5 x IQR rule) =", StatsEngine.outliers(email))
    220# Under the mean +/- 2 SD rule two runs are flagged: 48 and 51 minutes - the rule you choose changes the answer, so state it.
    221print("outliers (mean +/- 2 SD rule) =", StatsEngine.outliers_sd(email))

      Step by step — what the program does

      1. Set A. variance([8, 10, 9, 12, 11]) returns 2.5 and std_dev 1.581; the oracle statistics.stdev agrees, and pstdev (n) would give 1.414 — the number you must NOT see in a validation table.
      2. The trap. 0.1 + 0.2 == 0.3 prints False and the sum prints 0.30000000000000004; math.isclose(0.1 + 0.2, 0.3) prints True.
      3. Mode with ties. Counter(email) counts the 55 values; top is 5; the sorted list of the values with count 5 is [29, 32, 37]. The oracle statistics.multimode returns the same three values in order of first appearance.
      4. Spread. Variance 40.35, standard deviation 6.35 minutes, CV (coefficient of variation) 18.1 % (the ratio 0.181 printed with :.1%); the engine's SD compared with the oracle: == is False (6.352072224780001 vs 6.3520722247800006), isclose is True.
      5. Quartiles. at(0.25) finds position 13.5 → halfway between 30 and 31 → 30.5; at(0.75) → 39.5; statistics.quantiles(..., method='inclusive') prints the same three numbers.
      6. Fences and outliers. IQR (interquartile range) = 9; fences 17.0 and 53.0; outliers(email) is empty; outliers_sd(email) returns [48, 51] — two rules, two answers, one sentence to write in the notes.

      Task

      1# -*- coding: utf-8 -*-
      2# The module docstring: the economics engine with its guards, and the SQLite store that keeps the data.
      3"""CS 251 - Class 6 - Lesson 6.3: EconEngine with guards, and the Store (sqlite3 from the standard library).
      4
      5EconEngine: the formulas of Brick 3, each with a guard against an input that makes the formula meaningless.
      6Store: one tiny SQLite file (data/jarvis_demo.db here; data/jarvis.db in your project) that is created, filled
      7from the CSV (idempotently, thanks to a UNIQUE constraint), queried with GROUP BY, exported to CSV and vacuumed.
      8"""
      9
      10# closing() turns the connection into a context manager that CLOSES it at the end of the with block.
      11from contextlib import closing
      12# csv reads the dataset and writes the export file.
      13import csv
      14# math gives inf (an infinite payback when nothing is saved) and isclose (float comparison with a tolerance).
      15import math
      16# sqlite3 is the database engine of the standard library: no server, no installation, one file.
      17import sqlite3
      18# statistics is the oracle for the SQL average.
      19import statistics
      20# Path: relative paths only.
      21from pathlib import Path
      22
      23# The data folder, found from this file's location.
      24DATA_DIR = Path(__file__).resolve().parent.parent / "data"
      25# The CSV the Store imports.
      26CSV_PATH = DATA_DIR / "boreal_routines_2026.csv"
      27# The demo database file; the project's real file is data/jarvis.db.

      31# The economics engine: pure formulas, no state, so every method is static.
      32class EconEngine:
      33    # Class docstring: the three given numbers of the course are PARAMETERS of the methods, never constants inside them.
      34    """The formulas of Brick 3, each with a guard. Hourly value, prices and quotas are parameters, not constants."""
      35
      36    # The cost of a routine: minutes/60 x hourly value x runs.
      37    @staticmethod
      38    # routine_cost(35, 28, 100): 35 minutes a run, 28 $/h, 100 runs a month -> 1633.33 $.
      39    def routine_cost(minutes: float, hourly_value: float, runs: int = 1) -> float:
      40        # Docstring: the formula.
      41        """Cost of a routine: minutes / 60 * hourly_value * runs. Negative minutes or runs -> ValueError."""
      42        # Minutes and runs cannot be negative; a negative input is a data error, not a cost.
      43        if minutes < 0 or runs < 0:
      44            # Message with the offending values, so the caller can find the bad row.
      45            raise ValueError(f"minutes and runs must be >= 0, got {minutes} and {runs}")
      46        # The formula.
      47        return minutes / 60 * hourly_value * runs
      48
      49    # The opportunity cost of time spent by hand: what the same hours would earn in their next-best use.
      50    @staticmethod
      51    # opportunity_cost(35.15 / 60, 28): one manual e-mail run keeps 35.15 minutes from billable work worth 16.40 $.
      52    def opportunity_cost(hours: float, hourly_value: float) -> float:
      53        # Docstring: the formula and the guard.
      54        """Opportunity cost of hours spent by hand: hours * hourly_value. Negative hours -> ValueError."""
      55        # Hours cannot be negative; a negative input is a data error.
      56        if hours < 0:
      57            # Message with the value.
      58            raise ValueError(f"hours must be >= 0, got {hours}")
      59        # The formula.
      60        return hours * hourly_value
      61
      62    # The fixed cost of automation: the set-up time, paid once whatever the number of runs.
      63    @staticmethod
      64    # fixed_cost(40, 28): forty hours of set-up at 28 $/h = 1 120 $.
      65    def fixed_cost(setup_hours: float, hourly_value: float) -> float:
      66        # Docstring.
      67        """Fixed cost of the set-up: setup_hours * hourly_value (paid once; sunk once spent). Negative hours -> ValueError."""
      68        # Guard.
      69        if setup_hours < 0:
      70            # Message.
      71            raise ValueError(f"set-up hours must be >= 0, got {setup_hours}")
      72        # The formula.
      73        return setup_hours * hourly_value
      74
      75    # The variable cost of automation: the requests beyond the free quota, at the price per request.
      76    @staticmethod
      77    # variable_cost(3500, 3000, 0.02): 500 requests beyond the quota at 0.02 $ = 10 $ a month.
      78    def variable_cost(requests: int, free_quota: int, price_per_request: float) -> float:
      79        # Docstring: inside the quota the cost is 0.
      80        """Variable cost of the requests beyond the free quota: max(0, requests - free_quota) * price_per_request."""
      81        # Guard: a negative count of requests is a data error.
      82        if requests < 0:
      83            # Message.
      84            raise ValueError(f"requests must be >= 0, got {requests}")
      85        # Requests inside the quota cost nothing; max() keeps the count from going negative.
      86        return max(0, requests - free_quota) * price_per_request
      87
      88    # The total cost: fixed plus variable.
      89    @staticmethod
      90    # total_cost(1120, 10) = 1 130 $.
      91    def total_cost(fixed: float, variable: float) -> float:
      92        # Docstring.
      93        """Total cost: fixed + variable."""
      94        # The formula.
      95        return fixed + variable
      96
      97    # The marginal benefit of automating a routine.
      98    @staticmethod
      99    # MB = minutes saved per run / 60 x runs per month x hourly value.
      100    def marginal_benefit(minutes_saved: float, runs_per_month: int, hourly_value: float) -> float:
      101        # Docstring.
      102        """Marginal benefit per month: minutes_saved / 60 * runs_per_month * hourly_value."""
      103        # The formula; no guard needed beyond the ones of routine_cost's inputs, so it reuses routine_cost.
      104        return EconEngine.routine_cost(minutes_saved, hourly_value, runs_per_month)
      105
      106    # The average cost per run.
      107    @staticmethod
      108    # average_cost divides the total cost by the number of runs - impossible when there are no runs.
      109    def average_cost(total_cost: float, runs: int) -> float:
      110        # Docstring states the guard.
      111        """Average cost per run: total_cost / runs. Zero runs -> ValueError (no run, no average)."""
      112        # The guard: division by zero is not a number, it is a question the caller must answer.
      113        if runs <= 0:
      114            # Message.
      115            raise ValueError(f"average cost needs at least one run, got {runs}")
      116        # The formula.
      117        return total_cost / runs
      118
      119    # The break-even hours of a paid tier.
      120    @staticmethod
      121    # break_even_hours(20, 28): a 20 $/month tier pays for itself if it saves more than 20 / 28 = 0.714 h = 43 min a month.
      122    def break_even_hours(monthly_price: float, hourly_value: float) -> float:
      123        # Docstring states the guard too: an hourly value of zero (or less) makes the division meaningless.
      124        """Hours saved per month that pay for the tier: monthly_price / hourly_value. hourly_value <= 0 -> ValueError."""
      125        # The guard of the lecture: if hourly_value <= 0, raise.
      126        if hourly_value <= 0:
      127            # Message with the value.
      128            raise ValueError(f"hourly value must be > 0, got {hourly_value}")
      129        # The formula.
      130        return monthly_price / hourly_value
      131
      132    # The payback period of a set-up cost.
      133    @staticmethod
      134    # payback_months(1120, 910.86): a set-up of 1120 $ is recovered in 1.23 months of 910.86 $ net saving.
      135    def payback_months(fixed_cost: float, monthly_saving: float) -> float:
      136        # Docstring documents the decision: zero (or negative) saving -> infinity, not an exception.
      137        """Months to recover fixed_cost: fixed_cost / monthly_saving. Saving <= 0 -> math.inf (never recovered), documented."""
      138        # A set-up that saves nothing is never paid back: infinity is the honest answer, and it prints as 'inf'.
      139        if monthly_saving <= 0:
      140            # math.inf is a float, so the caller can still compare it with a budget of months.
      141            return math.inf
      142        # The formula.
      143        return fixed_cost / monthly_saving

      145
      146# The schema of the entries table (Appendix D of the schedule): one row per routine run, with a UNIQUE key.
      147SCHEMA = """
      148CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS entries (
      149  id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, date TEXT NOT NULL, staff_id TEXT NOT NULL, routine TEXT NOT NULL,
      150  category TEXT, start_hour INTEGER, minutes INTEGER NOT NULL CHECK (minutes >= 0),
      151  interruptions INTEGER DEFAULT 0, tool TEXT DEFAULT 'manual', done INTEGER DEFAULT 1,
      152  UNIQUE (date, staff_id, routine, start_hour));
      153"""
      154
      155
      156# The Store owns the database file: it is the only class that talks SQL.
      157class Store:
      158    # Class docstring.
      159    """The tiny SQLite store of JARVIS: create, import (idempotent), query, export, vacuum."""
      160
      161    # The constructor remembers the path and creates the tables if they do not exist yet.
      162    def __init__(self, path: Path) -> None:
      163        # The path of the .db file.
      164        self.path = path
      165        # Two context managers: closing(...) closes the connection at the end; 'con' commits on success, rolls back on error.
      166        with closing(sqlite3.connect(self.path)) as con, con:
      167            # executescript runs the whole schema string (several statements) in one call.
      168            con.executescript(SCHEMA)
      169
      170    # import_csv loads the CSV rows into the entries table; INSERT OR IGNORE skips a row that violates a constraint (UNIQUE, CHECK, NOT NULL) instead of raising.
      171    def import_csv(self, csv_path: Path) -> int:
      172        # Docstring: the return value is the number of rows in the table after the import.
      173        """Insert every row of the CSV; a row already present (same UNIQUE key) is ignored. Returns the row count."""
      174        # Open the CSV with the csv module's rules.
      175        with csv_path.open(newline="", encoding="utf-8") as f:
      176            # Each row becomes a tuple in the column order of the INSERT below; numbers converted from text.
      177            rows = [(r["date"], r["staff_id"], r["routine"], r["category"], int(r["start_hour"]), int(r["minutes"]),
      178                     int(r["interruptions"]), r["tool"], int(r["done"])) for r in csv.DictReader(f)]
      179        # One transaction for all the rows, and the connection closed afterwards.
      180        with closing(sqlite3.connect(self.path)) as con, con:
      181            # executemany runs the same INSERT once per tuple; the ? placeholders keep the values out of the SQL text.
      182            con.executemany("INSERT OR IGNORE INTO entries (date, staff_id, routine, category, start_hour, minutes, "
      183                            "interruptions, tool, done) VALUES (?, ?, ?, ?, ?, ?, ?, ?, ?)", rows)
      184        # The count after the import (all rows, not only the new ones): compare it with the count before to see what was added.
      185        return self.count()
      186
      187    # count returns the number of rows in entries.
      188    def count(self) -> int:
      189        # Docstring.
      190        """Number of rows in the entries table."""
      191        # A read-only query; fetchone() returns the first row of the result, a one-element tuple.
      192        with closing(sqlite3.connect(self.path)) as con:
      193            # [0] takes the number out of the tuple.
      194            return con.execute("SELECT COUNT(*) FROM entries").fetchone()[0]
      195
      196    # The GROUP BY query of the lecture: average minutes per routine and tool.
      197    def avg_minutes(self) -> list[tuple]:
      198        # Docstring.
      199        """(routine, tool, number of runs, average minutes) for every routine-tool pair, sorted."""
      200        # The query: GROUP BY collapses all rows with the same routine and tool into one row of aggregates.
      201        with closing(sqlite3.connect(self.path)) as con:
      202            # fetchall() returns every result row as a tuple.
      203            return con.execute("SELECT routine, tool, COUNT(*), AVG(minutes) FROM entries "
      204                               "GROUP BY routine, tool ORDER BY routine, tool").fetchall()
      205
      206    # The minutes of one routine and tool, straight from the table (used to compare SQL with Python).
      207    def minutes_of(self, routine: str, tool: str) -> list[int]:
      208        # Docstring.
      209        """The minutes column for one routine and tool, in insertion order."""
      210        # Parameters again with ?; never build SQL by gluing strings together.
      211        with closing(sqlite3.connect(self.path)) as con:
      212            # Each result row is a one-element tuple; the comprehension unpacks it.
      213            return [m for (m,) in con.execute("SELECT minutes FROM entries WHERE routine = ? AND tool = ? ORDER BY id",
      214                                               (routine, tool))]
      215
      216    # export_csv regenerates a readable copy of the table, so a reviewer can read the diff on GitHub.
      217    def export_csv(self, out_path: Path) -> int:
      218        # Docstring.
      219        """Write every row of entries to a CSV file (readable diffs in the repository). Returns the rows written."""
      220        # The folder of the export file may not exist yet.
      221        out_path.parent.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
      222        # Read all rows in id order.
      223        with closing(sqlite3.connect(self.path)) as con:
      224            # The cursor gives the rows; description gives the column names for the header line.
      225            cur = con.execute("SELECT * FROM entries ORDER BY id")
      226            # Column names come from the cursor's description.
      227            header = [d[0] for d in cur.description]
      228            # All the rows.
      229            rows = cur.fetchall()
      230        # Write the CSV with the csv module (newline="" is mandatory on Windows).
      231        with out_path.open("w", newline="", encoding="utf-8") as f:
      232            # A writer object.
      233            w = csv.writer(f)
      234            # Header first.
      235            w.writerow(header)
      236            # Then the rows.
      237            w.writerows(rows)
      238        # How many rows were exported.
      239        return len(rows)
      240
      241    # vacuum rebuilds the file so deleted space is returned - part of the tiny-database rule before every commit.
      242    def vacuum(self) -> None:
      243        # Docstring.
      244        """Rebuild the database file (reclaims free pages). Run before committing the file."""
      245        # VACUUM fails while a transaction is pending on the connection; isolation_level=None (autocommit) guarantees none is.
      246        con = sqlite3.connect(self.path, isolation_level=None)
      247        # The statement.
      248        con.execute("VACUUM")
      249        # Close explicitly: the connection is not in a with block here.
      250        con.close()
      251
      252    # size_bytes tells whether the file respects the 1 MB rule.
      253    def size_bytes(self) -> int:
      254        # Docstring.
      255        """Size of the database file in bytes."""
      256        # stat() asks the operating system; st_size is the size.
      257        return self.path.stat().st_size
      258

      260# --- EconEngine in action: the numbers of Class 3 -------------------------------------------------------------
      261# Break-even hours for the 20 $/user/month tier at 28 $/h: 0.714 h.
      262be = EconEngine.break_even_hours(20, 28)
      263# Printed in hours and in minutes (the owner thinks in minutes).
      264print(f"break-even: {be:.3f} h = {be * 60:.0f} min a month")
      265# Payback of a 40 h set-up (40 x 28 = 1120 $) with the net monthly saving of Brick 3 (910.86 $).
      266payback = EconEngine.payback_months(40 * 28, 910.86)
      267# Printed with two decimals.
      268print(f"payback: {payback:.2f} months")
      269# The documented edge case: nothing saved -> infinity, no crash.
      270payback_zero = EconEngine.payback_months(1120, 0)
      271# It prints as inf.
      272print("payback with zero saving:", payback_zero)
      273# The guard in action: hourly value 0 -> ValueError with the message of the engine.
      274try:
      275    # This call is refused by the guard.
      276    EconEngine.break_even_hours(20, 0)
      277# The exception arrives here.
      278except ValueError as error:
      279    # Print the message.
      280    print("hourly value 0 ->", type(error).__name__, "-", error)
      281# The monthly cost of manual e-mail triage: 35 min x 100 runs (5 staff x 20 days) at 28 $/h = 1633.33 $ (the board example of Class 3).
      282print(f"e-mail triage, 35 min x 100 runs: {EconEngine.routine_cost(35, 28, 100):.2f} $/month")
      283# The opportunity cost of one manual e-mail run: 35.15 minutes that could have been billed at 28 $/h.
      284print(f"opportunity cost of one manual e-mail run: {EconEngine.opportunity_cost(35.15 / 60, 28):.2f} $")
      285# Fixed cost of the set-up (40 h), variable cost of 3500 requests against a quota of 3000 at 0.02 $, total, average per run (100 runs).
      286fixed = EconEngine.fixed_cost(40, 28)
      287# The variable part: 500 requests beyond the quota.
      288variable = EconEngine.variable_cost(3500, 3000, 0.02)
      289# Fixed plus variable.
      290total = EconEngine.total_cost(fixed, variable)
      291# One line with the four numbers; the average cost is the total divided by the 100 runs of the month.
      292print(f"fixed {fixed:.2f} $ + variable {variable:.2f} $ = total {total:.2f} $ -> average per run (100 runs) {EconEngine.average_cost(total, 100):.2f} $")
      293# Marginal benefit of automating e-mail triage: 20.1 net minutes saved per run x 100 runs x 28 $/h / 60 = 938 $ a month.
      294print(f"marginal benefit (20.1 net min saved x 100 runs): {EconEngine.marginal_benefit(20.1, 100, 28):.2f} $/month")
      295
      296# --- The Store in action ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
      297# Start from nothing: delete the demo file if a previous run left it there, so every run is identical.
      298if DB_PATH.exists():
      299    # unlink deletes the file.
      300    DB_PATH.unlink()
      301# Create the store (and the entries table).
      302store = Store(DB_PATH)
      303# First import: 420 rows go in; the method returns the row count after the import.
      304rows_after_first = store.import_csv(CSV_PATH)
      305# Print it.
      306print("rows after import #1:", rows_after_first)
      307# Second import of the same file: every row hits the UNIQUE key and is ignored - still 420 (idempotent).
      308rows_after_second = store.import_csv(CSV_PATH)
      309# Print it: the same number.
      310print("rows after import #2:", rows_after_second)
      311# The GROUP BY result: 8 routine-tool pairs with their run counts and average minutes.
      312groups = store.avg_minutes()
      313# One line per pair.
      314for routine, tool, runs, avg in groups:
      315    # One line per pair; the same format specs you will use in the Reporter.
      316    print(f"{routine:<14}{tool:<9}{runs:>4} runs{avg:>8.2f} min")
      317# SQL and Python compute the same average from the same integers - compared with a tolerance anyway.
      318sql_avg = [a for r, t, n, a in store.avg_minutes() if r == "email_triage" and t == "manual"][0]
      319# The Python mean of the same 55 values, read back from the table.
      320py_mean = statistics.mean(store.minutes_of("email_triage", "manual"))
      321# isclose, not ==: floating-point sums can differ in the last digit depending on the order of the additions.
      322print(f"SQL AVG {sql_avg:.4f} vs Python mean {py_mean:.4f} -> isclose: {math.isclose(sql_avg, py_mean)}")
      323# Export for readable diffs.
      324print("exported rows:", store.export_csv(DATA_DIR / "export" / "entries.csv"))
      325# VACUUM before the commit, then the size check of the tiny-database rule.
      326store.vacuum()
      327# The size in bytes, asked once and kept.
      328size = store.size_bytes()
      329# Under 1 MB (1 048 576 bytes) by a wide margin: about 420 rows take a few dozen kilobytes.
      330print(f"database size: {size} bytes -> under 1 MB: {size < 1_048_576}")

        Step by step — what the program does

        1. The guards. break_even_hours(20, 28) returns 0.714 (43 minutes); payback_months(1120, 910.86) returns 1.23; payback_months(1120, 0) returns inf — a documented value. break_even_hours(20, 0) raises inside the method (watch the exception event) and the except branch prints the message.
        2. The other formulas. routine_cost(35, 28, 100) is 1 633.33 $ a month — the board example of Class 3 — then the opportunity cost of one run (16.40 $), fixed 1 120 $ + variable 10 $ = total 1 130 $, average 11.30 $ per run, and the marginal benefit of 938 $ a month.
        3. From nothing. If jarvis_demo.db exists it is deleted, so the run is reproducible; Store(DB_PATH) creates the file and the entries table from SCHEMA with executescript.
        4. Import twice. import_csv reads the CSV (Comma-Separated Values) into tuples, executemany inserts them with INSERT OR IGNORE; the count is 420 after the first import and still 420 after the second — the UNIQUE key did its job.
        5. GROUP BY. avg_minutes() returns eight tuples (routine, tool, runs, average); the loop prints them with :<14, :<9, :>4 and :>8.2f.
        6. SQL (Structured Query Language) vs Python. The e-mail average from AVG(minutes) and statistics.mean of the same 55 values read back with a ? parameter query are compared with math.isclose → True.
        7. Export, vacuum, size. export_csv writes 420 rows to data/export/entries.csv; vacuum() rebuilds the file (autocommit connection, closed explicitly); size_bytes() reports 53 248 bytes, under the 1 048 576-byte limit.

        Task
        The program reads the 420 rows, fills three defaultdict(list) groupings in one loop and prints a mean per routine with format specs; it then builds the validation table — 14 engine values against the numbers the Phase 1 scripts printed, each with a tolerance derived from the printed precision — counts the green rows, shows a deliberate red row (the bill with the pilot rows included), writes the table to CSV (Comma-Separated Values), checks the demo database against the 1 MB (megabyte) limit and ends with the two prediction lines of Activity 4.

        1# -*- coding: utf-8 -*-
        2# The module docstring: grouping with defaultdict, the validation table against the Phase 1 scripts, f-string report lines.
        3"""CS 251 - Class 6 - Lesson 6.4: grouping, the validation table and the console report.
        4
        5Grouping: defaultdict(list) collects the runs per routine, per staff member and per day in one pass.
        6Validation: every engine value is printed next to the value the Phase 1 scripts (Bricks 3 and 4) printed,
        7and the two are compared with a tolerance - this is the table of docs/validation.md (>= 8 green rows).
        8Report lines: f-strings with format specs (:<14 left-aligned text, :>10.2f right-aligned number, :.1% percentage).
        9"""
        10
        11# csv reads the dataset and writes the validation table.
        12import csv
        13# math.isclose compares floats with a tolerance; math.sqrt for the standard deviation.
        14import math
        15# defaultdict creates the list for a new key on first use, so grouping needs no "if key not in" test.
        16from collections import defaultdict
        17# Path for the relative paths.
        18from pathlib import Path
        19
        20# The data folder.
        21DATA_DIR = Path(__file__).resolve().parent.parent / "data"
        22# The dataset.
        23CSV_PATH = DATA_DIR / "boreal_routines_2026.csv"
        24# The demo database written by econ_store.py (Lesson 6.3) - checked here against the 1 MB rule.
        25DB_PATH = DATA_DIR / "jarvis_demo.db"
        26# The three given numbers of the course are parameters of the report, in one place.
        27HOURLY_VALUE = 28.0
        28# Runs per month per routine: 5 staff members x 20 working days (the convention of Brick 3).
        29RUNS_PER_MONTH = 100
        30
        31
        32# A compact copy of the engine methods used by the table (in your package they live in jarvis/stats_engine.py).
        33class StatsEngine:
        34    # Docstring.
        35    """The methods of Lessons 6.1 and 6.2 that the validation table needs."""
        36
        37    # mean: sum / count.
        38    @staticmethod
        39    # Empty list refused.
        40    def mean(xs):
        41        # Guard.
        42        if not xs:
        43            # Message.
        44            raise ValueError("mean of an empty list is undefined")
        45        # Formula.
        46        return sum(xs) / len(xs)
        47
        48    # median: middle of the sorted copy.
        49    @staticmethod
        50    # Sorted COPY, never in place.
        51    def median(xs):
        52        # Copy and sort.
        53        ordered = sorted(xs)
        54        # Count and middle index.
        55        n, mid = len(ordered), len(ordered) // 2
        56        # Odd count: the middle; even count: the average of the two middles.
        57        return ordered[mid] if n % 2 else (ordered[mid - 1] + ordered[mid]) / 2
        58
        59    # std_dev: square root of the sample variance (n - 1).
        60    @staticmethod
        61    # The sample convention of Class 4.
        62    def std_dev(xs):
        63        # The mean once.
        64        m = StatsEngine.mean(xs)
        65        # Squared deviations, divided by n - 1, under the root.
        66        return math.sqrt(sum((x - m) ** 2 for x in xs) / (len(xs) - 1))
        67
        68    # cv: std_dev / mean, a ratio.
        69    @staticmethod
        70    # Printed as a percentage by the caller.
        71    def cv(xs):
        72        # Ratio.
        73        return StatsEngine.std_dev(xs) / StatsEngine.mean(xs)
        74
        75    # quartiles: inclusive method, position (n - 1) * p with interpolation.
        76    @staticmethod
        77    # Returns Q1, Q2, Q3.
        78    def quartiles(xs):
        79        # Sorted copy and the last index.
        80        ordered, last = sorted(xs), len(xs) - 1
        81        # Inner helper for one quartile position.
        82        def at(p):
        83            # Position, lower index and fraction.
        84            pos = last * p
        85            # Lower neighbour.
        86            lo = int(pos)
        87            # Fraction of the gap.
        88            frac = pos - lo
        89            # Exact element, or interpolation between the two neighbours.
        90            return ordered[lo] if frac == 0 else ordered[lo] + frac * (ordered[lo + 1] - ordered[lo])
        91        # The three cut points.
        92        return at(0.25), at(0.5), at(0.75)
        93
        94    # outliers: the 1.5 x IQR rule.
        95    @staticmethod
        96    # Values outside the fences.
        97    def outliers(xs, k=1.5):
        98        # Quartiles.
        99        q1, _, q3 = StatsEngine.quartiles(xs)
        100        # Fences.
        101        low, high = q1 - k * (q3 - q1), q3 + k * (q3 - q1)
        102        # The flagged values.
        103        return [x for x in xs if x < low or x > high]
        104
        105
        106# One line of the economics engine is needed for the table (the full EconEngine is in econ_store.py).
        107def break_even_hours(monthly_price, hourly_value):
        108    # The guard of Lesson 6.3.
        109    if hourly_value <= 0:
        110        # Message.
        111        raise ValueError(f"hourly value must be > 0, got {hourly_value}")
        112    # Formula.
        113    return monthly_price / hourly_value
        114
        115
        116# Read the whole dataset once, converting the numeric columns.
        117with CSV_PATH.open(newline="", encoding="utf-8") as f:
        118    # One dict per row; minutes and done as integers.
        119    rows = [{**r, "minutes": int(r["minutes"]), "done": int(r["done"])} for r in csv.DictReader(f)]
        120
        121# --- Grouping with defaultdict: three dictionaries filled in ONE pass over the rows ------------------------------
        122# Key: routine -> list of minutes.
        123by_routine = defaultdict(list)
        124# Key: staff_id -> list of minutes.
        125by_staff = defaultdict(list)
        126# Key: date -> list of minutes.
        127by_day = defaultdict(list)
        128# One loop appends each row's minutes to the three groups it belongs to; a new key gets an empty list automatically.
        129for r in rows:
        130    # Group 1.
        131    by_routine[r["routine"]].append(r["minutes"])
        132    # Group 2.
        133    by_staff[r["staff_id"]].append(r["minutes"])
        134    # Group 3.
        135    by_day[r["date"]].append(r["minutes"])
        136# The three group counts: 6 routines, 5 staff members, 14 days.
        137print(f"groups: {len(by_routine)} routines, {len(by_staff)} staff, {len(by_day)} days")
        138# One report line per routine: name left-aligned in 14 characters, runs right-aligned in 4, mean right-aligned in 8 with 2 decimals.
        139for routine in sorted(by_routine):
        140    # The f-string with three format specs - the layout of the Reporter's console report.
        141    print(f"{routine:<14}{len(by_routine[routine]):>4} runs{StatsEngine.mean(by_routine[routine]):>8.2f} min")
        142
        143# --- The oracle values: what the Phase 1 scripts of Bricks 3 and 4 printed (Classes 3 and 4) ---------------------
        144# These numbers are the ones in docs/stats_notes.md and docs/econ_notes.md, with the number of decimals they were printed with.
        145ORACLE = {
        146    "mean, e-mail manual": (35.15, 2), "median, e-mail manual": (35.0, 2), "SD, e-mail manual": (6.35, 2), "CV %, e-mail manual": (18.1, 1),
        147    "Q1, e-mail manual": (30.5, 2), "Q3, e-mail manual": (39.5, 2), "IQR, e-mail manual": (9.0, 2), "outliers, 1.5 IQR": (0, 0),
        148    "mean, report before (manual)": (26.83, 2), "mean, report after (template)": (16.83, 2), "mean, e-mail pilot (jarvis)": (13.73, 2),
        149    "SD, standup (largest CV)": (2.62, 2), "break-even hours, 20 $ tier": (0.714, 3), "routine bill $/month": (5821.45, 2),
        150}
        151
        152# The minutes of the manual e-mail runs, the daily report before and after the template, and the pilot.
        153email = [r["minutes"] for r in rows if r["routine"] == "email_triage" and r["tool"] == "manual"]
        154# Daily report done by hand (days 1 to 7).
        155report_before = [r["minutes"] for r in rows if r["routine"] == "daily_report" and r["tool"] == "manual"]
        156# Daily report with the template (days 8 to 14).
        157report_after = [r["minutes"] for r in rows if r["routine"] == "daily_report" and r["tool"] == "template"]
        158# The 15 assistant-triaged e-mail runs.
        159pilot = [r["minutes"] for r in rows if r["routine"] == "email_triage" and r["tool"] == "jarvis"]
        160# The stand-up notes (the most variable routine of Class 4).
        161standup = [r["minutes"] for r in rows if r["routine"] == "standup_notes"]
        162# The routine bill of Brick 3: per routine, the mean minutes of the runs done without the assistant, x 100 runs x 28 $/h / 60.
        163bill = sum(StatsEngine.mean([r["minutes"] for r in rows if r["routine"] == name and r["tool"] != "jarvis"]) for name in by_routine) * RUNS_PER_MONTH * HOURLY_VALUE / 60
        164
        165# The engine values, in the same order as the oracle keys.
        166ENGINE = {
        167    "mean, e-mail manual": StatsEngine.mean(email), "median, e-mail manual": StatsEngine.median(email),
        168    "SD, e-mail manual": StatsEngine.std_dev(email), "CV %, e-mail manual": StatsEngine.cv(email) * 100,
        169    "Q1, e-mail manual": StatsEngine.quartiles(email)[0], "Q3, e-mail manual": StatsEngine.quartiles(email)[2],
        170    "IQR, e-mail manual": StatsEngine.quartiles(email)[2] - StatsEngine.quartiles(email)[0],
        171    "outliers, 1.5 IQR": len(StatsEngine.outliers(email)),
        172    "mean, report before (manual)": StatsEngine.mean(report_before), "mean, report after (template)": StatsEngine.mean(report_after),
        173    "mean, e-mail pilot (jarvis)": StatsEngine.mean(pilot), "SD, standup (largest CV)": StatsEngine.std_dev(standup),
        174    "break-even hours, 20 $ tier": break_even_hours(20, HOURLY_VALUE), "routine bill $/month": bill,
        175}
        176
        177# --- The validation table ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
        178# The header line, with the same widths as the rows below it.
        179print(f"\n{'method':<30}{'engine':>10}{'script':>10}  result")
        180# The rows of the table, kept for the CSV export.
        181table = []
        182# One row per method.
        183for name in ORACLE:
        184    # The engine value, the script value and the number of decimals the script printed.
        185    engine, (script, decimals) = ENGINE[name], ORACLE[name]
        186    # Tolerance = half a unit of the last printed digit: 0.005 for two decimals, 0.05 for one (the CV was printed as 18.1 %).
        187    ok = math.isclose(engine, script, abs_tol=0.5 * 10 ** -decimals)
        188    # The row of the report: name, engine value, script value, verdict.
        189    print(f"{name:<30}{engine:>10.3f}{script:>10.3f}  {'match' if ok else 'DIFFERENT'}")
        190    # Keep it for the file.
        191    table.append([name, round(engine, 4), script, "match" if ok else "DIFFERENT"])
        192# The count of green rows; Brick 6 asks for at least 8.
        193green = sum(1 for t in table if t[3] == "match")
        194# The verdict of the checkpoint.
        195print(f"green rows: {green} of {len(table)} (Brick 6 needs >= 8)")
        196
        197# --- Chasing a difference: a wrong rule shows up as a red row -------------------------------------------------
        198# The same bill computed with EVERY row, pilot runs included: a plausible formula, but not the one of Brick 3.
        199bill_all_rows = sum(StatsEngine.mean(by_routine[name]) for name in by_routine) * RUNS_PER_MONTH * HOURLY_VALUE / 60
        200# Printed next to the script value: the difference is not rounding, it is the rule (the pilot rows were excluded in Brick 3).
        201print(f"{'routine bill, pilot rows included':<34}{bill_all_rows:>10.2f}{ORACLE['routine bill $/month'][0]:>10.2f}  {'match' if math.isclose(bill_all_rows, ORACLE['routine bill $/month'][0], abs_tol=0.005) else 'DIFFERENT -> wrong rule, not rounding'}")
        202
        203# --- Export the table (docs/validation.md in your project; a CSV here) ---------------------------------------
        204# The folder.
        205(DATA_DIR / "export").mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
        206# Write with the csv module.
        207with (DATA_DIR / "export" / "validation.csv").open("w", newline="", encoding="utf-8") as f:
        208    # Header and rows.
        209    csv.writer(f).writerows([["method", "engine", "script", "result"]] + table)
        210# Confirm.
        211print("validation table written: data/export/validation.csv")
        212
        213# --- The tiny-database rule: the file of Lesson 6.3 must stay under 1 MB (1 048 576 bytes) ----------------------
        214# Only if econ_store.py was run first (it creates the demo file).
        215if DB_PATH.exists():
        216    # The size from the operating system.
        217    size = DB_PATH.stat().st_size
        218    # Size, share of the limit as a percentage, verdict.
        219    print(f"jarvis_demo.db: {size} bytes = {size / 1_048_576:.1%} of the 1 MB limit -> {'OK, commit it' if size < 1_048_576 else 'TOO BIG: is a plain INSERT import running on every start?'}")
        220# Otherwise say so instead of crashing.
        221else:
        222    # Message.
        223    print("jarvis_demo.db not found: run econ_store.py first")
        224
        225# --- Activity 4: predict these two lines before you run them ----------------------------------------------------
        226# Line 1: text left-aligned in 14, number right-aligned in 8 with 2 decimals, integer right-aligned in 5.
        227print(f"{'standup_notes':<14}{9.9143:>8.2f}{70:>5}|")
        228# Line 2: 3 decimals, a rounded integer, and a percentage with 1 decimal.
        229print(f"{20 / 28:.3f} h = {20 / 28 * 60:.0f} min | pilot/manual = {13.73 / 35.15:.1%}")

          Step by step — what the program does

          1. Reading. The CSV (Comma-Separated Values) becomes a list of 420 dictionaries; minutes and done are converted to int on the way.
          2. Three groupings, one loop. by_routine, by_staff and by_day are defaultdict(list); each row's minutes are appended to the three lists its keys select. The counts print as 6, 5 and 14, then one aligned line per routine.
          3. The oracle. ORACLE maps each method to the number the Phase 1 script printed and the number of decimals it printed; ENGINE holds the same keys with the engine's results, computed from the filtered lists.
          4. The table. For each key, math.isclose(engine, script, abs_tol=0.5 × 10^−decimals) decides match; the line is printed with :<30, :>10.3f, :>10.3f. Fourteen rows, fourteen matches — the CV (coefficient of variation) row only because its tolerance is 0.05.
          5. The chase. bill_all_rows prices every row, pilot included: 5 607.33 against 5 821.45 → DIFFERENT -> wrong rule, not rounding.
          6. Export and the size check. The table is written to data/export/validation.csv; jarvis_demo.db is 53 248 bytes = 5.1 % of the limit → OK, commit it.
